en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes 5.
The Training Rule on Receiving Robes.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā was staying at Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā dressed, took her bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after her meal and returning from her alms round, she went to the Blind Men’s Grove for her midday rest.
Having entered the Andhavana grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Now at that time, some thieves who had committed a robbery, having slaughtered a cow and taken its meat, entered the Andhavana grove.
There the village headman of the thieves saw the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā sitting at the foot of a certain tree for her midday rest.
Seeing him, it occurred to him:
"If my sons and brothers see this nun, they will harass her.
Thinking thus, he went by another path.

Then that village headman of thieves, when the meat was cooked, took some choice pieces, tied them in a leaf-wrapped bundle, and having hung it on a tree not far from the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, he said:
"Whatever ascetic or brahmin sees this, let him take what has been given," and then he departed.
The bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, having emerged from her concentration, heard those words spoken by the village headman of thieves.
Then the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā took that meat and went to her dwelling.
When that night had passed, the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā prepared the meat, tied it into a bundle with her upper robe, rose into the air, and alighted in the Bamboo Grove.
Now at that time, the Blessed One had entered the village for alms.
The Venerable Udāyī was left behind as the guardian of the monastery.
Then the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā approached the Venerable Udāyī and, having approached him, said this to him:
"Where, venerable sir, is the Blessed One?"
“The Blessed One has entered the village for alms, sister.
“Venerable sir, give this meat to the Blessed One.
“The Blessed One has been satisfied by you with the meat, sister.”
“If you would give me your inner robe, then I too would be satisfied by means of that inner robe.
“Venerable sir, we women are indeed those for whom gain is difficult to obtain. And this is my very last fifth robe;
I will not give it to you.”
“Sister, just as a man might give away an elephant and yet fasten his girth upon it,
even so, sister, having given the Blessed One your flesh, you are fastening your inner robe upon me. Then,
being thus pressured by the Venerable Udāyī, the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā gave him her inner robe and went to her dwelling place.
As the bhikkhunīs were receiving the bowl and robes from the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, they said to her,
“Where is your inner robe, noble lady?
The bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā explained the matter to the bhikkhunīs.
The bhikkhunīs complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the venerable Udāyī accept a robe from a bhikkhunī? Womenfolk are difficult to deal with!
Then those bhikkhunīs informed the bhikkhus of this matter.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the Venerable Udāyī accept a robe from a bhikkhunī?
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the Venerable Udāyī in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and so on].
“Is it true, Udāyi, that you accepted a robe from a nun?
“It is true, Blessed One.
“Is she a relative of yours, Udāyi, or is she not a relative?”
“‘She is unrelated to me, Blessed One.
‘Foolish man, one who is unrelated does not know whether [an action] is appropriate or inappropriate, or whether it is wholesome or unwholesome.
Yet you, foolish man, would accept a robe from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī!’”
“Foolish man, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
‘If any bhikkhu should accept a robe from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).’”
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, the bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept robes offered in exchange by bhikkhunīs.
The bhikkhunīs complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can it be that the noble ladies will not accept our exchanged robe?
The monks heard those bhikkhunīs grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Then the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this connection, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to accept an exchange from five persons—a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a female trainee, a male novice, and a female novice.
I allow you, bhikkhus, to accept an exchange from these five.”
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, however, a monk should accept a robe from the hand of an unrelated nun, except in exchange, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Whosoever, however...
Whoever such as this … [as above] … is a bhikkhu … [as above] …; this is the kind of bhikkhu intended in this context.
"One who is unrelated" means one who is not connected by blood on the mother’s side or the father’s side, up to the seventh generation of ancestors.
"Bhikkhunī" means...
One who is fully ordained in both Saṅghas.
"Robe" means any one of the six kinds of robes that is suitable for assignment and is of the lowest quality.
"Except by exchange" means excluding that which is obtained by exchange.
In the act of receiving it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By the mere acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.
It must be relinquished to either the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished:
… [as before] … Venerable sir, this robe-cloth was received by me from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī, except in exchange; it is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha. … [as before] …
"Should give" means ...
"should give" means ...
"I give to the Venerable One."

If he accepts a robe from a woman who is not related to him, perceiving her as one who is not related, except in exchange, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If he accepts a robe from a woman who is not related to him, being doubtful of her relationship, except in exchange, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If he accepts a robe from a woman who is not related to him, perceiving her as one who is related, except in exchange, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one receives a robe from the hand of a fully ordained woman, except in exchange, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is a relative but one perceives her as not being a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is a relative but one is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is a relative and he perceives her as such, there is no offense. There is no offense if she is a relative.
If a monk takes an exchange— whether for a small amount he gives a large one, or for a large amount he gives a small one—
or if he takes it on trust,
or takes it for a limited time;
Having set aside the robe-cloth, one takes another requisite belonging to a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerī).
"Of one who is insane,
of one who is a first-time offender.
The fifth training rule concerning the acceptance of robes is finished.
